title: The Lark and Her Chick
intro: In the 1898 preface to his Diwan, Shawqi recalls reading his fables to young Egyptians and taking heart when they understood them at once and laughed. Here a mother lark gives her chick a flying lesson, choosing a branch beside hers and giving him time to rest between flights. Shakib Arslan quotes all ten couplets as an example of Shawqi’s plain language. Al-Waaedh repeats the last couplet, in which the narrator weighs seizing a moment against missing it.

translation: In one of the gardens I saw a lark
teaching her chick to fly in a treetop.
1.sharh: This teller claims to have seen the lesson himself. The verb for flying has been turned into a verb for making another fly, so the mother is a teacher from the first line.

translation: She was saying, “Beauty of the nest,
don’t put your trust in a tender wing.
2.sharh: “Beauty of the nest” is what the chick means to her. “Tender” is a separate, practical judgement on the wing he is about to put to work.

translation: Perch on a twig beside another.
Do as I do when you climb.”
3.sharh: A twig beside hers gives him both a landing place and a close view of the next move. She teaches by example before she lets him attempt open air.

translation: She moved from branch to branch,
giving every move its time,
4.sharh: The same word for a bough sounds twice, like two successive perches of much the same height. Time, as carefully allotted as distance, is part of the lesson.

translation: so the chick could rest between flights
and not grow weary of the weight of air.
5.sharh: The phrase gives air an unexpected weight. A learner’s wing feels the labour of staying aloft in something that seems weightless to a watcher on the ground.

translation: But he disregarded her signal,
wanting to show how clever he was.
6.sharh: The chick’s purpose has shifted from learning to giving a display. What he imagines as cleverness looks rather different to the witness who tells the story.

translation: He flew into the open, climbing high.
His wing let him down, and down he fell.
7.sharh: The wing itself seems to break faith with him. The verbs that carry him up and let him fall end on the same open vowel, a quick rise and an equally quick reversal.

translation: Both knees broke on the spot.
Of all the heights he hoped for, none was his.
8.sharh: The strangely precise tally of injuries makes the little body visible. “The heights” can also mean distinction, exactly what the bird hoped his exploit would win.

translation: Had he taken his time he’d have won his wish
and lived at ease all his days.
9.sharh: The poem briefly allows the chick the future his mother could see for him. The long life she was preparing for throws the single disastrous jump into relief.

translation: Everything in life has its time.
Those who rush only end up missing it.
10.sharh: Waqtuhu, its time, answers fawtuhu, its being missed. The two closely related sounds leave the listener with the small interval between using a moment and losing it.

1.1.4.head: الرِّياض
1.1.4.meaning: Gardens or green meadows, the setting in which the speaker saw the birds.

1.1.5.head: قُبَّرَة
1.1.5.meaning: A lark, a small songbird. The related Arabic name qunbura also occurs.

1.2.1.head: طَيَّرَ
1.2.1.meaning: Made another fly or taught it to take wing.

2.1.4-5.head: جَمال العُشّ
2.1.4-5.meaning: “Beauty of the nest”, the mother’s pet name for her chick.

2.2.2.head: اِعتَمَدَ
2.2.2.meaning: Relied on something to bear one’s weight, a literal possibility for the fledgling’s wing.

2.2.5.head: الهَشّ
2.2.5.meaning: Frail or tender, here a wing too weak for sustained flight.

3.1.5.head: عود
3.1.5.meaning: A twig used as a perch. Both diwans print “twig” without a final y. Sustaining the rhyme can also make it sound like “my twig”, the mother’s own perch.

4.1.3.head: فَنَن
4.1.3.meaning: A bough or branching limb of a tree.

4.2.3.head: نَقلَة
4.2.3.meaning: One move or transfer from perch to perch.

4.2.4.meaning: An interval deliberately allowed between movements. Arslan quotes thaman, a price or cost.

5.1.3.head: الفَرخ
5.1.3.meaning: A chick or fledgling that has yet to master flight.

5.2.3-4.head: ثِقَل الهَواء
5.2.3-4.meaning: “The weight of air”, the strain of keeping a young body aloft.

6.1.4.head: الإِشارَة
6.1.4.meaning: The mother’s direction, given both in words and by the example of her movement.

6.2.4.head: الشَّطارَة
6.2.4.meaning: Cleverness or dash, here something the chick is eager to show off.

7.1.5.head: اِرتَفَعَ
7.1.5.meaning: Rose into the air. The final a is drawn out in rhyme, as it is in “fell” in the next half. Both verbs describe the one chick.

7.2.1.head: خانَ
7.2.1.meaning: Failed someone at the crucial moment, as though the wing were a companion who had broken faith.

8.2.4.meaning: The heights of achievement, with the literal height above the ground still in view.

9.1.2.meaning: Took time, waited for the right moment.

9.2.4.meaning: At ease or blessed with a pleasant life. The ending of muhanna’ is eased in rhyme.

10.2.1.head: غايَة
10.2.1.meaning: The end one reaches, here the ironic outcome of losing what one set out to gain.

10.2.3.head: فَوت
10.2.3.meaning: The loss of an opportunity before one can grasp the thing desired.
